newsitem.title: UK: British budget to avoid health, spending cuts.
newsitem.headline: British budget to avoid health, spending cuts.

text.p: The UK government will look to cut public spending at next week's budget but the sacred political cows of health and education are sacrosanct and will not be touched, analysts said on Friday.

Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke will want to balance any tax cuts he makes in the budget for fiscal 1997/8 with planned spending reductions to produce a budget at least nominally neutral in fiscal terms.

Most economists expect Clarke -- who is under heavy pressure to help the ruling Conservations get re-elected next year -- to unveil tax cuts of around 3.0 billion pounds ($5.05 billion). He must find around the same amount in spending cuts. First target will be the government's so-called contingency reserve -- a fund maintained for unforeseen emergencies. Adam Cole, UK economist at James Capel, said the government could cut as much as 2.5 billion pounds from next year's reserve even though compensation paid out for the "mad cow" crisis this year has eaten into funds already.
"The obvious target is the contingency reserve," Cole said, adding that with a bit of juggling, Clarke could actually increase spending on health and education.
The rest of the money that has to be made up would probably come out of infrastructure purses, Cole said.
"As usual, the axe will fall first on capital spending. That gives benefits straight away and you don't feel the pain for years afterwards."

Alissa Goodman, research economist at influential thinktank the Institute for Fiscal Studies, agreed that looming elections ruled out spending cuts for the National Health Service or education system. A general election must be held by May 1.

"It's a lot easier, politically, to not build a road or houses, than to sack teachers or cut the number of hospital beds." She added that the government may look to rein in spending in areas where the Public Finance Initiative and National Lottery were directing resources.

The PFI is a government initiative to encourage private sector involvement in major infrastructure projects. "There could be cuts in investment programmes in a number of departments, particularly housing and roads -- all the things where the PFI is expected to come in and fill the gap," Goodman said.
The National Lottery, meanwhile, has proved a roaring success with the British public and has started to shell out for various heritage-type projects.
"With both the PFI and lottery, the government said any investment would be in addition to, not instead of public spending. But that does not sound plausible," Goodman said.
Cole said Clarke's get-out-of-jail card was the improvement in Britain's public sector borrowing requirement, which is the official budget deficit.
The government got an unexpected bonus on Monday when figures were released showing tax revenues outstripped government expenditure by a massive 4.4 billion stg in October.
Most economists had been expecting a public sector debt repayment of no more than two billion.

A Reuter poll of 27 London-based economists, conducted on Thursday, showed Clarke is expected to slice one billion pounds off his 26.9 billion stg forecast for this year's PSBR and two billion off the 23 billion target for 1997/98 when he announces his budget on Tuesday.
That could allow him to pull off a budget hattrick of a cut in the basic rate of income tax, lower PSBR forecasts and spending increases in the most politically sensitive areas.

But Kevin Gardiner, UK economist at Morgan Stanley said real spending cuts were needed. "A little bit will come out of the contingency reserve but the most important thing is to get departmental spending room down," he said.

Gardiner said there was still slack to be tightened in government spending. "It's crazy to pay child benefit to families who don't need it, for example. I'm not suggesting they will change that but that is the sort of area that can be addressed."
Gardiner feared Clarke may cut tax credits on company dividends paid out to shareholders. That would be poison for the stock market.
"If they attack tax credits on share dividends they might not have to reduce spending too much, but they really should be addressing that side of the equation," he said. ($1=.5940 Pound)
